Suppose half the sampled cells are malignant, every cell has two local copies, and each affected cancer cell carries one altered copy, with equal recovery per copy. Then VAF = purity times cancer-cell fraction divided by two; 0.20 = 0.50 times CCF divided by two gives CCF 80 per cent. With pure cancer-cell input, the same 20 per cent fits CCF 40 per cent. These are model calculations, not counted cells. Local copy changes, altered-copy multiplicity, recovery bias or uncertain purity can change the fit. In a fictional TP53 example, 60 cancer cells each carry one variant copy and have lost the other local copy; 40 normal cells each have two unaltered copies. With equal recovery per copy, the expected variant fraction is 60 divided by 140, about 43 percent. Another model, 86 percent cancer-cell purity with two local copies and one variant copy in every cancer cell, gives 86 divided by 200, exactly 43 percent. Both round to 43 percent when reported to a whole percentage point. That reported fraction alone cannot choose the copy model or establish that a missense variant disables the protein. These are conditional calculations, not a measured clone or a functional test.

Two invented mixtures show why the same fraction can fit different carrier fractions. Each contains 60 cancer and 40 diploid normal cells, with no variant in the normal cells and unbiased recovery. Model A gives every cancer cell two local copies and one variant copy: 60 variant copies among 120 cancer plus 80 normal copies give VAF 30 percent and CCF 100 percent. Model B gives every cancer cell four local copies, with 48 of the 60 cells carrying two variant copies each: 96 among 240 cancer plus 80 normal copies again give VAF 30 percent, but CCF is 80 percent. They match that one fraction; they have not been shown to fit the same complete dataset. Independent copy evidence can distinguish the hypotheses.

In a separate invented uniform-copy model, 50 cancer and 50 normal cells each carry two local copies; normal cells lack the variant and each carrier cancer cell has one variant copy. Among 200 total copies, an expected VAF of 20 percent requires forty carriers among fifty cancer cells, or CCF 80 percent. An expected VAF of 40 percent would require eighty carriers among fifty, or 160 percent, which is not a possible carrier fraction. Preserve that incompatibility rather than clipping it to 100 percent or guessing which input is wrong. The calculation inverts an expected fraction; noisy observed support and uncertain purity, copy number, multiplicity, origin or recovery require their uncertainty carried through. More reads can improve precision without fixing a wrong model.

Barroso-Sousa and colleagues analysed 3,969 primary or metastatic breast-cancer samples from six public studies using exome or panel sequencing. Median mutation burden differed across their receptor-defined groups, with the triple-negative group above HER2-positive and hormone-receptor-positive/HER2-negative groups. The study's research threshold belongs to its analysis and does not replace a later label or another assay's rule.

Lung cancer is where tumour mutational burden was discovered as a predictor of checkpoint benefit (Rizvi 2015) and where it failed as a selector. The biology holds: burden tracks outcome within every PD-L1 stratum in 1,552 patients and is independent of PD-L1 (Rizvi 2018, Ricciuti 2022). The measurement does not: three units are in use (per megabase on a panel, per exome on sequencing, a plasma score), the best data-derived threshold was more than 19 per megabase rather than the licensed 10, and the association vanishes entirely once chemotherapy is added to the checkpoint inhibitor (Garassino 2023). It selects for single-agent immunotherapy only (Mok 2023).

changes.before: A targeted panel sequences only a chosen set of a few hundred cancer genes, deeply and cheaply, which is what most hospitals run on tumours today.
changes.after: A targeted sequencing panel examines selected DNA regions. Its exact targets, analysed change types and detection limits depend on the assay.
changes.reason: Replace unsupported fixed gene-count, cost and hospital-usage generalizations with the validated subject definition.

changes.before: Exome sequencing works by selecting a subset of DNA before sequencing (Wikipedia); a targeted panel narrows the selection further to hundreds of clinically relevant genes, read at high depth from small samples. Panels such as MSK-IMPACT and FoundationOne underlie AACR Project GENIE, the largest clinico-genomic dataset, but panel coverage differs between institutions, so pooling requires restricting to shared genes and treating unsequenced genes as missing rather than wild type.
changes.after:
A targeted panel sequences a predefined set of genomic regions, ranging from particular hotspots to broader gene sets. Selected introns or other noncoding regions can be included when the intended analysis requires them. The panel name or gene count alone does not establish which variants can be detected or how much usable evidence exists at a position.

When combining results from different panels, an unsequenced region supplies no wild-type observation. Compare the actual tested regions, analysed change types and specimen-specific performance before pooling records or interpreting a negative result.
changes.reason: Correct the definition and preserve the missing-versus-wild-type reading rule. The named GENIE aside and unsourced largest-dataset ranking are intentionally omitted from this definition, not certified false; the existing link and relationships remain.

after: A panel can target selected non-exon regions as well as coding sequence. Exome designs primarily target exons, which include sequence retained in mature RNA that need not encode protein; genome designs sample coding and noncoding territory more broadly. Each design can leave important positions without usable evidence. Keep intended coordinates, local depth, filters and validated alteration classes together; breadth alone does not rank sensitivity or clinical usefulness.
